description: UN Security Council Resolution 1267 (1999) established the Al-Qaeda Sanctions Committee. Updated by UNSCR 1989 (2011, splitting into two lists) and UNSCR 2253 (2015, adding ISIS/ISIL). Maintained as the consolidated list with asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo.

UN Security Council Resolution 1718 (2006) established the DPRK sanctions regime after nuclear test. Subsequent resolutions (1874, 2087, 2094, 2270, 2321, 2371, 2375, 2397) significantly expanded: coal/iron/seafood export ban, oil import cap, financial sector restrictions.

UN Security Council Resolution 1737 (2006) established UN sanctions on Iran's nuclear and ballistic missile programmes. UNSCR 2231 (2015) endorsed JCPOA and provided snapback mechanism. UN sanctions partially suspended under JCPOA 2016-2019, then US withdrew from JCPOA (2018).

UN Security Council Resolution 2140 (2014) establishing targeted sanctions against individuals and entities threatening peace in Yemen. Asset freeze and travel ban. Panel of Experts monitors implementation.

UN Security Council Resolution 1970 (2011) establishing arms embargo, asset freeze, and travel ban against Libyan regime. Referred matter to ICC. Subsequent resolutions modified and expanded the regime.

UN Security Council targeted financial sanctions require immediate freezing of funds and economic resources owned, held, or controlled by designated individuals and entities. Member states must implement without delay — same-day implementation expected under FATF R.6.

UN Security Council travel bans prohibit entry to or transit through territories of member states by designated individuals. Member states may grant exemptions for humanitarian or religious purposes. Must be transposed into national law.

UN Security Council arms embargo prohibiting supply, sale, or transfer of arms and military equipment to embargoed countries or designated entities. Member states must ensure national export control laws prohibit violations.

Financing of the development, production, or acquisition of weapons of mass destruction (nuclear, chemical, biological, radiological). FATF R.7 requires countries to implement TFS against CPF (primarily DPRK and Iran). Separate risk assessment requirement from ML/TF.

Weapons of mass destruction and related materials including: nuclear materials (U235, Pu239), chemical precursors, biological agents, delivery systems (ballistic missiles). International controls under IAEA, CWC, BWC, and NSG.

Process for adding individuals/entities to UN sanctions lists: (1) Proposal by member state; (2) Sanctions Committee review (no formal vote — silence procedure); (3) Addition to list published. Delisting: submitted through Ombudsperson (for 1267 list) or focal point. Due process concerns significant.

Independent position established by UNSCR 1904 (2009) to review delisting requests from individuals on the Al-Qaeda/ISIS sanctions list. The Ombudsperson reviews requests and provides non-binding recommendations to the Sanctions Committee. Addresses due process concerns.

Process by which member states implement UN Security Council sanctions: legislation (sanctions act, executive order), designation of competent authority, publication in national register, financial institution notification, enforcement mechanism. EU implements via EU regulations.

FATF Recommendation 6 and its Interpretive Note require countries to implement UN TFS without delay (same-day for preventive purposes). Specific requirements: legislative authority, competent authority designation, FI notification mechanism, prohibitions on public/private sectors.

FATF Recommendation 7 requires countries to implement UNSCR 1718 and 1737 TFS without delay. High-risk indicator: countries with DPRK or Iran correspondent banking relationships. CPF risk assessment required separately from ML/TF under Recommendation 7.

The EU implements UN Security Council sanctions through EU Council regulations. EU often adds autonomous measures exceeding UN obligations (e.g., Russia/Ukraine). EU consolidated list includes both EU autonomous measures and UN sanctions as implemented in EU law.

FATF Recommendations 6 and 7 operationalise the UN Security Council TFS obligations for the financial sector. FATF Mutual Evaluations assess whether countries implement UNSCR 1267 and 1718 effectively. High deficiencies trigger enhanced follow-up.

AMLR Art. 6 requires obliged entities to comply with targeted financial sanctions including UN-derived TFS. Obliged entities must screen against UN sanctions lists (as implemented in EU law). Sanctions match requires both asset freeze AND SAR filing.

Known DPRK sanctions evasion methods: ship-to-ship transfers of oil/coal on the high seas; front companies in China and Southeast Asia; cryptocurrency theft by state-sponsored hacking groups (Lazarus Group); labour export disguised as workers; false flags and ship identity fraud.

Known Iran sanctions evasion methods: use of front companies in Turkey, UAE, and China; oil tanker identity manipulation; petrodollar recycling through gold and currency markets; access to USD through European correspondent banks (pre-2018).
